newsitem.title: BELGIUM: US farm bill seen as transatlantic bargaining tool.
newsitem.headline: US farm bill seen as transatlantic bargaining tool.

text.p: United States farm trade negotiators, justified by successful U.S. farm reform, would keep a close eye on European competitors in world food markets, retired U.S. Agriculture Department official Gene Moos said.
"We don't intend to initiate the use of unfair trade practices with the interest of gaining market share," he said.
"But we will certainly be prepared to respond to unfair competition if other major exporters use such patterns."
Moos was talking to Reuters during the Lipidex 97 oilseeds conference and stressed his views were individual and did not officially represent USDA or Clinton administration thinking.
One of the key architects of the 1995 U.S. farm bill, Moos left his post as USDA under-secretary last December.
"As a strong proponent of liberalised trade, we hope (distortions) won't happen," Moos said.
He thought EU export policy had done a good job managing wheat trade flows, avoiding excessive subsidy levels.
And budgetary pressures and the prospect of eastward enlargement should support adjustment moves in the future which would bring EU export subsidies in line with world market prices.
Likewise, expanding global oilseeds demand and rising prices might entice EU producers to drop long-standing demands to renegotiate a bilateral trade accord limiting the oilseeds area.
"I'm not sure how the political pressure will evolve regarding the need to renegotiate it (the so-called Blair House deal agreed in 1992)," Moos said.

Remaining contentious trade issues were the EU ban on the output boosting meat hormone BST and outstanding mandatory clarification from the EU on how it was implementing certain GATT round stipulations in barley and some other markets.
Moos said the full transition to market-driven production choices in the U.S. caused concern over farmers' abilities to fully and profitably respond to growing world food demand.
With stocks at their lowest levels in 20 years, U.S. production was the only means of responding to demand while crop supply depended entirely on unpredictable weather patterns.
"There'll be substition between different crops reflecting market signals, which will create risks and price volatility, but it will also allow farmers to make efficient choices."
Moos also said there were calls to raise the U.S. minimum public grains reserves from less than three million to the required four million tonnes and perhaps beyond.
In his speech to the conference, Moos said EU farm policy was lagging U.S. efforts to do away with farmer support and crop control by 10 or 15 years.
Futures hedging and crop insurance programmes were now replacing income support and excessive stockholding.
Prices of more than $8 per bushel of soybeans had caused a shift of acreage into oilseeds this season from a more corn-oriented 95/96 season, showing the new freedom was working.
Moos also said he was optimistic on oilseeds demand as Asian livestock industries were growing.
China had more than doubled its per-capita annual meat use to 44 kg over the last 10 years.
